1.title: BusControl QR
1.description: Multi-role mobile app for municipal school transport: QR attendance with an offline queue, a live bus map, and push notifications for families, backed by Supabase.
1.motivation: School municipal transport attendance used to be manual and easy to lose, and parents had no way to know if their kid boarded or where the bus was. I wanted to solve both sides at once: a reliable log for the driver and assistant (QR plus offline fallback), and real-time visibility for families.
1.overview: BusControl is an Expo/React Native app backed by Supabase, with separate roles for driver, assistant, parent, and coordinator. Driver and assistant log attendance by QR even without signal (the app syncs on its own once connection is back); parents see their kids and the bus on a live map and get push notifications on every event.
highlights: Multi-role app: driver, assistant, parent, and coordinator in one codebase
Offline attendance queue that syncs on its own once the connection is back
Live bus map and push notifications for families
Business rules (attendance, priority, permissions) covered by unit tests and CI on every push
1.approach: I split business rules (attendance, priority, role permissions) into a UI-free domain layer so they could be unit-tested with Jest without booting the app, key to not breaking attendance tracking when I added the offline queue. For the bus map, I chose native Apple Maps on iOS and OpenStreetMap via WebView on Android/web, to avoid depending on a paid Google Maps API key on a municipal project with a tight budget. For trip state I used React's own useSyncExternalStore instead of adding Zustand or Redux: the app already loads camera, maps, and push, and I didn't want another dependency for something React already solves. Lint and tests also run automatically on GitHub Actions on every push.
learnings: Designing testable business rules separate from the UI
Handling offline/optimistic state without losing attendance events
Coordinating different roles (driver, parent, coordinator) over the same data domain

2.title: TypingPro
2.description: Web platform to practice typing speed with texts filterable by type, difficulty and language, user accounts, and a global leaderboard. Next.js frontend and NestJS/Prisma backend.
2.motivation: I wanted a project that exercised a stack split into two real applications, a Next.js frontend and a NestJS API with its own database, authentication, and admin panel, instead of another single-framework full-stack project.
2.overview: TypingPro measures typing speed and accuracy over texts filterable by type (quote, article, code, paragraph), difficulty, and language. Each typing session is saved against the user's account, feeding a global leaderboard and notifications. A separate admin panel manages the available texts, languages, and difficulty levels.
highlights: NestJS backend with Prisma, JWT authentication, and an admin guard kept separate from the rest of the API
Text filtering by type, difficulty, and language consumed from the frontend
Global leaderboard computed from saved typing sessions
Admin panel to manage texts, languages, and difficulties
2.approach: I split the project into two applications (Next.js for the UI, NestJS for the API) instead of a full-stack monolith, to version and test the business logic (WPM calculation, ranking, admin permissions) independently from the UI. In the backend I used Prisma as the data access layer and organized each domain (auth, texts, typing sessions, leaderboard, notifications, admin) into its own NestJS module with its own tests, instead of one large controller. The admin guard lives apart from the regular auth guard so role permissions don't get mixed with session validation.
learnings: Designing a NestJS API organized by domain modules instead of a monolith
Separating authentication from authorization (session guard vs. admin role guard)
Modeling typing sessions and aggregating them into a consistent global leaderboard
